findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — Limit Shortfall vs. Maricopa $5M Requirement
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include, but not be limited to; coverage for all directors, officers, agents and employees of the Contractor, losses with respect to network risks (such as data breaches, unauthorized access or use, and ID theft of data), invasion of privacy (regardless of the type of media involved in the loss of private information), crisis management, identity theft response costs, breach notification costs, credit remediation, and credit monitoring, defense, and claims expenses, regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration expenses (data asset protection), network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction, and loss outside the premises of the named insured.
findings.policy_quote: Aggregate Limit of Liability: $4,000,000 ... DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY. THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY AVAILABLE TO PAY LOSS AND THE RETENTION SHALL BE REDUCED AND MAY BE EXHAUSTED BY THE PAYMENT OF DEFENSE COSTS.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa contract demands $5,000,000 per occurrence Cyber. AmTrust policy provides only $4,000,000 aggregate (NOT per-occurrence) shared across 14 coverage lines, with Defense Within Limits eroding the aggregate. After typical 60-80% defense erosion on a major breach, effective indemnity capacity is $800K–$1.6M — roughly 16-32% of the contracted minimum. No excess Cyber tower exists; Hanover Umbrella has absolute Cyber Incident, Data Privacy, and Access/Disclosure exclusions on both Coverage A and B (475-0654, 475-0655, 475-0661) so it cannot drop down.
findings.plain_english: Your contract with Maricopa County requires $5 million of cyber coverage per claim. You have $4 million total — and that pot has to pay your lawyers, forensic experts, and PR firm before it pays a single dollar to the County. After defense costs eat through the policy (typical for any serious breach), there's roughly $1 million left to actually pay damages. You're not just under the contract limit on paper; the real, usable coverage is closer to one-fifth of what Maricopa demanded. There is no umbrella above your cyber policy — your umbrella explicitly excludes cyber. This is the single largest exposure in your program.
findings.recommendation: Immediately bind a Cyber excess tower of at least $5M xs $4M to bring the program to $9M total — given a single ransomware event in election technology can easily exceed $10M, $5M of additional Cyber capacity is the floor. Simultaneously negotiate (a) defense outside limits or (b) separate sublimit dedicated to defense on the renewal. Notify Maricopa procurement under §8.2.15 of any material change. Long-term: shop the entire Cyber tower at renewal — election technology is a high-demand class and admitted markets are now writing $5M+ per occurrence.
discoveryQuestions: If a ransomware crew encrypted your ballot processing systems three weeks before the November election, walk me through how you'd respond — and where do you think the money to fund that response actually comes from?
Have you ever modeled what a notification event for 90 million voters would cost you in just notification, credit monitoring, and forensic costs — before you defend a single lawsuit?
When you signed the Maricopa contract did anyone confirm to you, in writing, that your $4M cyber policy satisfies the $5M-per-occurrence requirement? Because as written, it doesn't.
Your umbrella has a hard cyber exclusion — were you aware that there's no excess tower above your primary cyber policy at all?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Cyber Deception / Social Engineering Phantom Coverage
findings.contract_quote: ...funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction...
findings.policy_quote: Cyber Deception (Social Engineering): Limit $250,000 / Retention $250,000
findings.gap_description: Cyber Deception sublimit is $250,000 with a $250,000 retention — meaning on any single social engineering loss, the insured pays the first $250K, then the carrier pays the next $250K maximum. Effective recoverable on any loss ≤$250K is exactly $0; on a $500K loss the recovery is $250K (50%); on a $1M loss the recovery is still $250K (25%). For an election services company processing county invoices, refund disbursements, and vendor payables, this is phantom coverage. Hartford Crime sublimit for Deception Fraud / Social Engineering is also only $15,000 — together the social-engineering capacity across the entire program is $265K limit / $250K retention.
findings.plain_english: If a bad actor poses as a county procurement officer and tricks your AP team into wiring $400,000 to a fraudulent account, your policy structure is set up so you eat the first $250,000 yourself, and the most you can ever recover is another $250,000 — leaving you out the rest. Smaller loss? You recover nothing. This isn't underinsurance — it's the appearance of coverage with the dollars structurally unable to reach you.
findings.recommendation: At renewal, demand restructured Cyber Deception coverage: at minimum $1M limit with $25K-50K retention as separate from the aggregate. As an interim measure, consider a Crime policy upgrade (Hartford Crime currently $15K social engineering — far worse). Also implement enhanced wire-transfer verification controls (out-of-band callback, dual approval at $25K threshold) — many carriers will increase limits at no premium increase if controls are documented.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hartford Mgmt Liability Crime Part — Deception Fraud sublimit $15,000 (also inadequate)
discoveryQuestions: Walk me through what happens when a county sends you a payment instruction change request — who verifies it, and how?
Have any of your peer election services companies been hit by wire fraud in the last 24 months? What did they recover?
Did you know that on a $300K wire-fraud loss, your current cyber policy pays you exactly $50K — and on anything under $250K, you recover zero?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Missing Additional Insured / Waiver of Subrogation / Designated Entity NOC
findings.contract_quote: The insurance policies required by this contract, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall name County, its agents, representatives, officers, directors, officials, and employees as additional insureds. ... The policies required hereunder, except Workers' Compensation and Errors and Omissions, shall contain a waiver of transfer of rights of recovery (subrogation) against County... Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: [No Additional Insured endorsement, no Waiver of Subrogation endorsement, and no Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation endorsement appears in the AmTrust Cyber policy. Item 8 Endorsements list on the Dec page is blank in the available excerpt.]
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's §8.2.7 explicitly carves out only WC and E&O from the AI requirement — Cyber IS required to name County as AI. Same for WoS (§8.2.8) and 30-day notice of cancellation/material change (§8.2.15). The Cyber policy contains none of these endorsements. This is a triple uncured contract breach as of policy inception 4/1/2025.
findings.plain_english: Your Maricopa contract is explicit: every policy except Workers Comp and E&O must (1) name the County as an additional insured, (2) waive subrogation against the County, and (3) give the County 30 days notice if anything material changes on the policy. Your Cyber policy has none of these three. If a covered cyber claim arises, the County could declare you in material breach, and AmTrust could quietly subrogate against the County after paying you. The contract was signed; the endorsements were never built.
findings.recommendation: Immediately request from AmTrust: (1) AI endorsement listing Maricopa County (note: many cyber forms cannot accommodate AI status — if AmTrust will not endorse, escalate to procurement for written waiver or seek replacement market that will), (2) Blanket Waiver of Subrogation for written contracts, (3) 30-day Designated Entity NOC listing Maricopa County, Sacramento County, and Los Angeles County. If AmTrust refuses any of the three, this is a leverage point at renewal — there are admitted Cyber markets that will provide all three without negotiation.
discoveryQuestions: When you signed the Maricopa contract, who confirmed that your Cyber policy actually names the County as an additional insured?
If the County asks for a current Cyber COI showing AI status and 30-day notice, what document do you have to give them today?
Is your broker aware that §8.2.7 requires AI on Cyber and not just on GL/Auto?

findings.requirement_type: D&O — Manufacturing and Professional Services Exclusion (Hartford)
findings.contract_quote: (N/A — D&O is not contractually required, but is a board-level exposure for a PE-backed company.)
findings.policy_quote: EXCLUSION FOR MANUFACTURING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICE ENDORSEMENT — Insurer shall not be liable to make any payment for Loss based upon, arising from, or in any way related to: (1) any malfunction of any product or product failure, including any deficiency, inadequacy, defect or dangerous condition in any product or its design or manufacture; or (2) the actual, alleged or threatened rendering or failure to render any services for fees, including services for customers or clients of an Insured Entity.
findings.gap_description: Hartford Private Choice Premier D&O endorsement bars coverage for any claim arising from product malfunction OR rendering/failure to render any services for fees. For an election technology services firm whose ENTIRE BUSINESS is rendering printing/mailing/processing services for fees to county clients, this exclusion eviscerates the most likely claim scenarios — counties suing for negligent service delivery, election errors, mail-handling failures. Only carve-backs are securities-holder civil proceedings and Derivative Actions. Side C (Entity Liability) is effectively unavailable for the operational risk profile that drives this company.
findings.plain_english: Imagine the worst-case scenario: a county loses a close election, blames Run-Test for late-arriving ballots, files suit against the company AND its directors for negligent oversight. Your Hartford D&O policy excludes that claim — entirely. The exclusion bars coverage for any claim 'arising from rendering or failure to render any services for fees.' That's literally what you do. The only D&O claims that ARE covered are securities/shareholder suits and shareholder derivative actions — the things that almost never happen at a private PE-backed company. You are paying $41,564 for a D&O tower that, in practical terms, doesn't respond to your real operational risk.
findings.recommendation: Aggressively shop D&O at renewal — multiple carriers (Chubb, AIG, Travelers, Beazley) will write D&O for an election technology firm without the Manufacturing/Professional Services exclusion. If Hartford insists, demand carve-back language for: (a) county/government client claims arising from contract performance, (b) claims involving regulatory investigation of election services. Document this exclusion to the board immediately — directors should know their personal liability exposure for entity-level claims is effectively uninsured for core operations.
discoveryQuestions: If a county loses a close election and sues you and your directors personally for negligent oversight of ballot processing, who at Run-Test is reading the D&O exclusion language?
Has your PE sponsor (Lincoln Shields / Black Mountain) reviewed the entity-liability gap on your D&O? Most sponsors require 'manufacturing-exclusion-free' D&O for portfolio companies.
What is the worst-case operational claim scenario your board worries about — and have you confirmed it would be covered, not excluded, on the current D&O?

findings.requirement_type: GL Limits Shortfall vs. Maricopa $2M Occurrence / $4M Aggregates
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Each Occurrence Limit: $1,000,000 ... General Aggregate Limit: $2,000,000 ... Products-Completed Operations Aggregate: Included in General Aggregate (NOT a separate limit) ... Aggregate Limits of Insurance Per Project and Per Location With Cap — Total Aggregate Cap: $2,000,000.
findings.gap_description: Hanover primary GL is $1M/$2M with Products-Completed Ops INCLUDED in (not separate from) the General Aggregate, plus a $2M Policy Aggregate Cap on the per-project/per-location aggregate endorsement (421-3635). Maricopa requires $2M occurrence / $4M general aggregate / SEPARATE $4M Products-Completed Ops aggregate. Maricopa §8.2.9 expressly permits umbrella stacking, so the $10M Hanover Umbrella does cure the each-occurrence shortfall (combined $11M each occurrence). However, neither the umbrella schedule nor the GL policy provides a separate Products-Completed Ops aggregate at the contract level, and the $2M policy aggregate cap on per-location/per-project means the underlying GL provides only $2M general aggregate regardless of project count.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires $2 million per claim, $4 million total per year, AND a separate $4 million bucket dedicated only to claims that arise after a project is finished. Your primary GL gives you $1 million per claim, $2 million total, with no separate finished-projects bucket. The $10 million umbrella sitting on top fills in the per-claim gap, but the structure on paper still doesn't match what Maricopa demanded. If a county's risk manager pulls your COI and reads the limits literally, this is the kind of administrative defect that gets flagged.
findings.recommendation: (1) Increase Hanover primary GL to $2M each occurrence / $4M general aggregate / $4M separate PCO aggregate at renewal — the cost differential is typically modest. (2) Remove or raise the $2M policy aggregate cap on form 421-3635 — the per-project/per-location aggregate is meaningless when capped at $2M total. (3) Re-issue Maricopa COI documenting the umbrella stack so the County's reading of the per-occurrence limit is unambiguous.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella UH4 H221416 05 ($10M each occurrence, $10M PCO agg, $10M Gen Agg) — Coverage A follows form over GL; combined tower $11M satisfies per-occurrence and aggregate minimums
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa's risk manager ever pushed back on a COI showing $1M GL each occurrence, even when the umbrella stacks above it?
On your largest current contract, what's your worst-case product liability exposure if a defective ballot caused a recount or election challenge?
Did you know your per-project aggregate is capped at $2M total — meaning if you have a bad year on one county contract, every other county shares the same $2M pool?

findings.requirement_type: GL — Cyber/Data Privacy/BIPA Exclusions Conflict with Maricopa 'No Additional Exclusions' Mandate (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: Insurance Services Office's Commercial General Liability occurrence coverage form CG 0001. Including, but not limited to Premises/Operations, Products/Completed Operations, Contractual, and Personal & Advertising Injury, without additional exclusions or limitations, unless approved by the County Risk Manager.
findings.policy_quote: Exclusion — Cyber Incident — Cyber Content (421-5286 01 25); Exclusion — Violation Of Law Addressing Data Privacy (CG 00 69 12 23); Exclusion — Access Or Disclosure Of Confidential Or Personal Material Or Information (CG 21 06 12 23); Exclusion — Phthalates (421-5203 07 23); Exclusion — PFAS (CG 40 32 05 23); Total Pollution Exclusion (CG 21 49 09 99); Silica Exclusion (CG 21 96 03 05); Fungi/Bacteria (CG 21 67 12 04).
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §II.A requires CG 0001 'without additional exclusions or limitations, unless approved by the County Risk Manager.' Hanover GL has at least eight non-standard exclusion endorsements layered on top of CG 00 01 — three of which (cyber incident, data privacy, access/disclosure) are highly material to an election-services contractor handling 90M+ voter records. Three overlapping cyber exclusions create what is effectively a complete cyber/privacy carve-out from GL; combined with the Hanover Umbrella's matching cyber/data privacy/access-disclosure exclusions (475-0654, 475-0655, 475-0661), the entire liability tower has zero cyber-tort coverage. Sacramento has not approved any of these exclusions on the record provided.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento's contract is unusually strict — it says 'use the standard ISO general liability form, no extra exclusions, period.' Your Hanover GL is built on the standard form, but the carrier added eight non-standard exclusions on top, including three that strip out any cyber or data-privacy claim. For a company that handles voter data for 90 million Americans, those three exclusions carve out exactly the kind of claim a county would bring against you. Sacramento's risk manager hasn't approved them. If a Sacramento contract goes wrong on the cyber side, you risk both a coverage denial AND a contract breach claim.
findings.recommendation: (1) Submit the full GL endorsement list to Sacramento County Risk Manager with explanation of each non-standard exclusion and request explicit approval (or carve-back). (2) At renewal, push Hanover to remove the redundant pollution exclusions (CG 21 49 AND CG 21 55 are both attached and conflict — flag for cleanup). (3) Confirm cyber exposures are fully transferred to the standalone Cyber tower (which itself is undersized — see finding-001).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Stand-alone AmTrust Cyber policy is the only line responding to cyber claims, and that policy is undersized for the contractual minimum (see finding-001)
discoveryQuestions: When you sent your COI to Sacramento, did you also send the full endorsement list — or just the certificate?
If a county sues you for a data privacy claim under California's CCPA or CPRA, walk me through which policy responds — and what the limit looks like after defense costs.
Are you aware that your GL has three separate cyber-related exclusions stacked on top of each other?

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine — No Policy in Program / Sacramento WoS Required If In Force
findings.contract_quote: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: [No Inland Marine policy was provided in the program submission.]
findings.gap_description: Run-Test transports ballots, election equipment, and high-value sorters/scanners between its Phoenix facility and county election sites across 31 states. The Hanover Commercial Property has Property Off-Premises ($250K) and BPP In Transit ($100K) sublimits — meaningfully inadequate for the actual operations. The Auto policy explicitly excludes care/custody/control of cargo (CA 00 01 §II.B.2.h). There is NO standalone Inland Marine policy or Motor Truck Cargo policy in the program. Cargo loss in transit (a stolen ballot truck, a fire in a sorter shipment, hijacked vehicle) is therefore essentially uninsured beyond the $100K sublimit. Separately, Sacramento's WoS requirement only triggers IF an IM policy is in force — it currently is not, so the contractual trigger is dormant, but the underlying exposure is severe regardless.
findings.plain_english: You move ballots, mail, and high-value election equipment around the country. Your auto policy will pay if your driver hits another car — but it will NOT pay for the ballots, equipment, or property in your truck if it's lost, stolen, or destroyed in an accident. Your property policy covers $100,000 of stuff in transit, period. A single sorter line is worth more than that. A truckload of unprocessed ballots stolen on the way to a county is potentially catastrophic — operationally, financially, and reputationally. There is no insurance for that loss on this program.
findings.recommendation: Bind a standalone Inland Marine / Motor Truck Cargo policy immediately. Recommended structure: (a) $1M-$5M per conveyance, (b) blanket coverage for ballots, election supplies, sorters, scanners, and printing equipment in transit, (c) blanket WoS endorsement (satisfies Sacramento §IX trigger), (d) coverage at named sub-locations during temporary deposit. Cost is typically modest relative to coverage. This is a missing-policy gap, not an underwriting problem.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Commercial Property has only $100K BPP in Transit and $250K BPP Off Premises sublimits — well below typical truckload value
discoveryQuestions: What's the highest-value truckload of ballots or equipment you've ever shipped — and what's the most expensive piece of mail-sorting equipment you'd lose if a delivery truck caught fire?
If a truck carrying a sorter line is hijacked or destroyed, where do you think the money to replace that equipment comes from?
Have any of your peer election services companies had a transit loss recently? How did it resolve?

findings.requirement_type: Auto Limit Shortfall vs. Maricopa $2M CSL
findings.contract_quote: Commercial/Business Automobile Liability insurance with a combined single limit for bodily injury and property damage of not less than $2,000,000 each occurrence with respect to any of the Contractor's owned, hired, and non-owned vehicles assigned to or used in performance of the Contractor's work or services or use or maintenance of the premises under this contract.
findings.policy_quote: Liability Combined Single Limit: $1,000,000
findings.gap_description: Hanover primary Auto is $1M CSL; Maricopa demands $2M CSL. The Hanover Umbrella's Coverage A follows form over the underlying Auto and provides $10M, so the combined tower ($11M) far exceeds the contracted minimum. However, Maricopa §8.2.11 (the Auto-specific clause) does NOT inline-mention umbrella attachment — only §8.2.9 (the program-level umbrella permission clause) does. Strict reading of §8.2.11 alone leaves the $1M primary short of $2M; permissive reading per §8.2.9 cures with umbrella stack.
findings.plain_english: Your auto policy gives you $1 million per accident; Maricopa demands $2 million. Your $10 million umbrella sits on top and follows form for auto, so practically you're at $11 million combined. Most counties accept umbrella-stacked totals, but Maricopa's contract language for auto specifically doesn't mention umbrella in the auto clause — and a strict reading would say you're short. Worth raising the underlying limit to $2M to remove the ambiguity entirely.
findings.recommendation: Raise Hanover Auto primary CSL to $2M at renewal — incremental premium is generally $500-2,000 for a fleet this size. This removes the strict/permissive interpretation question and aligns underlying limits with the Maricopa minimum without requiring the umbrella to fill the gap.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Umbrella UH4 H221416 05 — Coverage A follows form over Auto with $10M each occurrence
discoveryQuestions: If Maricopa's risk manager reads your COI literally and demands $2M on the auto line not stacked with umbrella, what's your timeline to fix?
What's the cost differential to raise the primary auto from $1M to $2M? Most carriers charge under $2K for a fleet your size.
Are any of your Maricopa drivers involved in higher-risk operations — long hauls, late-night deliveries during election cycles?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber Continuity Date vs. Maricopa Retro-Date Requirement
findings.contract_quote: In the event that the insurance required is written on a claims-made basis, Contractor warrants that any retroactive date under the policy shall precede the effective date of this contract and either continuous coverage will be maintained, or an extended discovery period will be exercised for a period of two years beginning at the time work under this contract is completed.
findings.policy_quote: Continuity Date: April 1, 2023.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's contract serial 220121-IGA / 220141-IGA was effective 11/01/2021. The Cyber policy continuity date is 4/1/2023 — eighteen months AFTER the contract effective date. Any latent cyber incident with a 'first cause' between 11/01/2021 and 4/1/2023 (a persistent threat actor, an undiscovered breach, an unreported privacy violation) is uncovered. Run-Test has 50+ years of operating history; long-tail cyber exposures predating 2023 are foreseeable. Both Sacramento (§V.A) and Maricopa (§8.2.3) require retro to precede the contract effective date — this policy fails that test for the Maricopa contract.
findings.plain_english: Your Maricopa contract started in November 2021. Your cyber policy only covers events that took place after April 2023. That 18-month gap is uninsured. If a state-actor breach started in your network in 2022 and only got discovered today, your cyber policy will deny — and the Maricopa contract terms are violated. For a 50-year-old company with election-data exposure, that retroactive gap should not be there.
findings.recommendation: At Cyber renewal, demand a retro date of at least 11/01/2021 (Maricopa contract effective) — and ideally an unlimited or 'inception' retro date given the 50-year operating history. Many cyber markets will agree to extended retro for a small premium increase. Concurrently provide written disclosure to Maricopa procurement under §8.2.3 if the retro cannot be moved before the next renewal cycle.
discoveryQuestions: When did Run-Test first encounter a cyber incident — even a minor one — that you're aware of?
If a state-sponsored actor had been in your network since 2022 and you discovered it tomorrow, walk me through which policy responds.
Did your Maricopa contract due-diligence check whether your cyber retro date predated the contract effective date?

findings.requirement_type: Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation — Maricopa County NOT Listed
findings.contract_quote: Applicable to all insurance policies required within the insurance requirements of this contract, Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: WC Designated Entities: El Paso County, Coconino County, Amazon. ... Auto Designated Entities: Blanket where required by written contract, City of Boulder, Coconino County, Amazon.com Services LLC, El Paso County Contracts & Procurement Division, San Luis Obispo County, State of Colorado, NY State Office of General Services. ... GL Designated Entities: NY State OGS, Amazon.com Services LLC, ARC Airport 2800 LLC, Banterra Bank.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa County is not on any Designated Entity Notice of Cancellation schedule across the WC, Auto, GL, Cyber, Umbrella, or E&O policies. While the Auto NOC schedule includes a 'BLANKET WHERE REQUIRED BY WRITTEN CONTRACT' line which arguably picks up Maricopa, the WC and GL NOC schedules are limited to specifically named entities and Maricopa is absent. Cyber has no DENOC at all. Standard ACORD COI 'in accordance with policy provisions' language (typically 10 days) does not satisfy Maricopa §8.2.15's 30-day requirement.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires their procurement office to receive 30 days' notice if any of your policies cancel or change. Your policies have notice schedules listing some other counties (Coconino, El Paso, etc.) — but Maricopa isn't on any of them. The COI you sent likely says 'we'll give you whatever notice the policy provides,' which on most policies is 10 days for non-payment. That's a contract breach waiting to be flagged on audit.
findings.recommendation: Submit endorsement requests to Hanover (WC, Auto, GL, Umbrella) and AmTrust (Cyber) to add Maricopa County, c/o Risk Management, 301 W Jefferson St Suite 910, Phoenix AZ 85003 to the Designated Entity NOC schedule with 30-day notice. Also add Sacramento County and Los Angeles County while updating. Hanover policies already have the form mechanism (331-0342 WC / 401-1235 Auto-GL); just expand the schedule.
discoveryQuestions: When was the last time your broker confirmed which county procurement offices are on your policy NOC schedules?
If your cyber policy were canceled mid-term for non-disclosure, who would Maricopa hear from — and when?
Has any county ever audited your COI compliance and pushed back on the cancellation notice clause?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Mgmt Liability — Prior Acts Cutoff & Split P&P Date
findings.contract_quote: (N/A — D&O not contractually required, but PE-backed company exposure.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #28 (PP 00 H033) Prior Acts Exclusion: 'Excludes Claims based upon, arising from or related to any Wrongful Act prior to 8/18/2023, or Interrelated Wrongful Acts thereto.' Endorsement #34 (PP 00 H105) Split Prior or Pending Date: '04/02/2024 applies ONLY to the additional/increased $1,000,000 layer in excess of the first $1,000,000.'
findings.gap_description: Two compounding restrictions: (1) absolute prior-acts cutoff of 8/18/2023 across D&O, EPLI, and Fiduciary — only one year of prior acts coverage despite 50-year operating history; (2) split P&P date creates a 'donut' on the upper $1M D&O layer for matters pending between 8/18/2023 and 4/2/2024. For a PE-backed company with heightened regulatory and shareholder scrutiny, the narrow prior-acts window is a meaningful gap.
findings.plain_english: Your management liability policy only covers wrongful acts from August 2023 forward — anything that happened before then, even if you only got sued for it last week, is excluded. For a 50-year-old company, that's a tight window. There's also a quirky structure where the upper half of your D&O limit (the second $1M) has a different start date than the lower half — meaning a matter pending between August 2023 and April 2024 is covered by only $1M, not the full $2M. Both are PE-driven underwriting features and worth pushing back on at renewal.
findings.recommendation: At renewal: (1) negotiate prior-acts back to at least the date PE sponsors Lincoln Shields/Black Mountain acquired their interest, (2) collapse the split P&P date so both layers attach on the same day, (3) shop the management liability tower across two or three markets to see what 'unlimited prior acts' looks like in pricing. PE sponsors typically require longer prior-acts windows on portfolio company D&O.
discoveryQuestions: When did Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain acquire their stake — and was the prior-acts date set to that closing date?
Has Run-Test ever had a regulatory matter that surfaced years after the underlying event? Election-services class actions sometimes have decade-long latency.
Did your PE sponsors review the D&O prior-acts construction before close?

findings.requirement_type: E&O — Delay-in-Performance Exclusion Conflicts with Time-Critical Election Work
findings.contract_quote: (General contractual obligation to perform on time — Maricopa Exhibit B §2.1.3 requires F.O.B. destination delivery; election deadlines are statutory and immovable.)
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #6 D. Exclusions ADDED — 'Any actual or alleged delay in performance or delivery of any Technology Products or services or any contractual or other duty.'
findings.gap_description: Endorsement #6 (Technology Services Extension) adds a Delay-in-Performance exclusion to Gemini's E&O. Election work is fundamentally time-critical — ballots that arrive after election day are useless, and counties suffer hard statutory deadlines. A delay claim is foreseeable and an obvious heads of damages on this risk profile, yet Endorsement #6 expressly excludes it. The Convex excess sits over Gemini and follows form (or 'more restrictive') so this exclusion flows up the entire $10M tower.
findings.plain_english: If a county sues you because ballots showed up late and the election was disrupted, your professional liability policy will likely deny the claim — there's a delay exclusion baked in. For an election services company, claims of 'late delivery' are the most foreseeable type of professional services dispute that exists. The exclusion was almost certainly added when the carrier extended technology services coverage to your policy, but it doesn't fit your business model.
findings.recommendation: Aggressively negotiate removal or carve-back of the Endorsement #6 D delay exclusion at renewal. Position language: delay caused by Insured's negligence in performing professional services should remain covered; only delay caused by force majeure or third-party logistics failure should be excluded. Multiple election-services-specialty E&O markets (Coalition, Beazley, Tokio Marine HCC) write election technology E&O without a flat delay exclusion.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had a near-miss — ballots that almost didn't make the deadline? What did the county say?
If a county sues you for missing a statutory mail-by date, who at Run-Test reads the policy first?
Walk me through the language in your county contracts about timing — and tell me how that interacts with this exclusion.

findings.policy_quote: Convex Dec page Item 5: Followed Policy 'Gemini Insurance Company VIPL056495.' Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301, Page 13): 'Gemini Insurance Company VIPL055885.'
findings.gap_description: Two different Gemini policy numbers cited on the same Convex excess policy — one on the Dec page and a different number on the Schedule of Underlying. The Gemini primary in the program is VIPL056495. If a coverage dispute arose and the schedule reference doesn't match the actual underlying, Convex could argue the wrong underlying is scheduled (a maintenance-of-underlying defense).
findings.plain_english: Your $5M excess E&O policy says it sits over Gemini policy VIPL056495 on the front page, but on page 13 it lists VIPL055885 — a different policy number. Just an administrative defect, but in a coverage dispute it's the kind of typo a carrier could try to wiggle out on. Easy fix.
findings.recommendation: Request endorsement from Convex correcting the Schedule of Underlying Insurance to match the Dec page (VIPL056495). Five-minute administrative fix.

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Verify P&NC and AI Follow Form for Maricopa
findings.contract_quote: Maricopa §8.2.7 requires AI on Umbrella; §8.2.4 requires P&NC; §8.2.8 requires WoS.
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella checklist: additional_insured_blanket: false, primary_noncontributory: false, waiver_of_subrogation: false. [These boxes show false in the analysis JSON because the umbrella relies on follow-form rather than standalone endorsements.]
findings.gap_description: Umbrella does not contain standalone AI/P&NC/WoS endorsements; it relies on Coverage A follow-form to the underlying GL and Auto. This is standard but Maricopa §§8.2.4-8.2.8 require these features on each required policy — including Umbrella as a required policy. Strict reading: umbrella needs its own AI/P&NC/WoS endorsements; permissive reading: follow-form satisfies. Needs written confirmation from Maricopa procurement.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella inherits the AI, P&NC, and WoS features from the GL and auto by following form — that's standard insurance practice. But Maricopa's contract language treats the umbrella as a separate required policy and demands these features on it directly. Most counties accept follow-form; Maricopa's literal reading might not. Worth getting written confirmation.
findings.recommendation: (1) Submit written request to Maricopa procurement confirming follow-form satisfies AI/P&NC/WoS requirement on Umbrella, OR (2) request standalone Umbrella AI/P&NC/WoS endorsements from Hanover (typically nominal premium). Document either resolution path.
discoveryQuestions: Has Maricopa risk management ever asked for the umbrella to specifically endorse AI/P&NC?
What does your COI show for the umbrella line?

findings.requirement_type: Cyber — Defense Within Limits + Shared Aggregate Compounding
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa demands per-occurrence $5M cyber; this policy structure makes effective per-event capacity far less.)
findings.policy_quote: All 14 coverage lines (Ransom, Data Recovery, Bricking, BI, BI from Suppliers, Reputation Harm, Cyber Event, Cyber Deception, Proof of Loss, Cryptojacking, Privacy & Network Security, Regulatory Fines, Payment Card, Media) share the single $4M aggregate. ... DEFENSE COSTS ARE PART OF AND NOT IN ADDITION TO THE AGGREGATE LIMIT OF LIABILITY.
findings.gap_description: The combination of (1) shared aggregate across 14 coverages, (2) defense within limits, and (3) the underlying $4M aggregate (vs. $5M required) creates a stacked coverage failure. A single ransomware event hitting both Ransom Payment ($1M paid) AND Data Restoration ($1M) AND BI ($500K) AND Defense ($1.5M) erodes the entire $4M in one event with zero capacity remaining for any other claim during the policy period — including a regulatory action that could follow the breach. Effectively, every dollar of one cyber loss can trigger the cap on every other cyber coverage.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy has a structural problem that compounds the $4M-vs-$5M shortfall. Every type of cyber claim — ransom, data restoration, business interruption, regulatory defense, social engineering, payment card — draws from the same $4M bucket. Defense costs come out of that bucket. So a single ransomware event could exhaust the entire policy mid-claim, leaving you uninsured for the regulatory and class action that follows the breach. This is by far the most fragile coverage architecture in your program.
findings.recommendation: (1) Bind Excess Cyber to add $5M-$10M of capacity above primary. (2) At renewal, demand defense outside of limits — admitted markets routinely offer this for a 5-10% premium uplift. (3) Demand sub-aggregates by coverage line to prevent single-event total depletion. (4) Negotiate per-occurrence rather than aggregate-only limits where possible.
discoveryQuestions: If a single cyber event triggered ransom + data recovery + BI + regulatory defense at the same time, walk me through how the $4M lasts.
Have you ever seen a peer in election technology actually use this kind of policy in a claim?
Has anyone modeled what 'defense within limits' looks like on a real claim — typically 60-80% of the limit gone before settlement?
